paper_title: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A single prompt often asks language model to do several things at once, such as answering handful of questions, solving set of math problems, or following list of instructions before writing one response. Common benchmarks, however, still test models one task at time [Rein et al., 2023, Hendrycks et al., 2021, Gema et al., 2025]. As scores on these benchmarks saturate, they may overstate how robust the underlying capabilities are. We ask whether model that reliably solves task on its own can still solve it when other tasks share the prompt. One natural explanation is error accumulation. If each task fails with nonzero probability, solving many at once fails more often. Prior work has found this phenomenon when models are tasked to do familiar reasoning steps [Press et al., 2023, Dziri et al., 2023, Sinha et al., 2026] or follow several instructions at once [Harada et al., 2025, Vasileva, 2026]. However, accumulation is only half of the story. Because composition in these settings also changes the structure and token demands of the task, it remains unclear whether the models ability to solve each constituent task degrades as well, and what mechanism drives that degradation. To investigate the question, we analyze the effect of composition on each constituent task of composition. We start by establishing that this per-task degradation exists at all. For that, we select tasks the model solves correctly in isolation, which establishes that the requisite capability is present. We then leave those tasks unchanged and simply concatenate them within single prompt. This design separates degradation under increased task load from baseline solvability on the constituent tasks. Across state-of-the-art open models, as well as the frontier model Claude Opus 5, we find substantial performance degradation when more previously solved tasks are concatenated within the same prompt. The drop in accuracy is substantially larger than what the constituent tasks isolated error rates would predict, and is consistent across both mathematical and linguistic domains. We characterize this degradation along two dimensions. 1) Failures concentrate on subset of fragile tasks that, for given model, remains stable across sampling noise and composition sizes. These tasks also have longer reasoning traces in isolation. 2) As more tasks are presented together, models systematically reduce the reasoning tokens devoted to each task, even though no explicit per-task token constraint is imposed. This reduction follows clear scaling pattern, with reasoning per task decreasing approximately as power law with composition size. Together, these findings reveal an implicit thinking budget under composition, under which fragile tasks disproportionately lose accuracy as per-task reasoning decreases. This mechanism also creates an opportunity for more efficient inference than solving every task separately. Non-fragile tasks can be grouped into larger batches, where the implicit thinking budget reduces per-task reasoning and token usage without impacting accuracy. Fragile tasks, in contrast, are placed in smaller batches so that each receives more reasoning and remains accurate. We demonstrate this with fragility-aware batching, strategy that composes each task based on its fragility. By using empirical measurements of the fragility of tasks, it reduces token usage by 43% on average with no drop in performance compared to solving each task individually. Because it is entirely black-box, it also applies directly to proprietary models, reducing generated tokens by 24% on GPQA-Diamond with Claude Opus 5 without degrading performance. Taken together, these results show that the failure of LLMs to generalize their reasoning budget management is double-edged sword. Under composition, it causes fragile tasks to fail, whereas in isolation, it makes models overspend reasoning on non-fragile tasks, thus wasting compute during inference. Our key contributions and findings are: We show that simply concatenating tasks that are already solved correctly in isolation causes substantial accuracy degradation across both frontier and open models (Section 3). We identify an implicit per-task thinking budget that shrinks as power law in the number of 2 composed tasks (Section 3.1). We show that this uniform reduction concentrates degradation on tasks with long isolated reasoning, set that is stable within each model but differs between models (Sections 3.1 and 3.2). We refer to this set of tasks as fragile. We turn these findings into fragility-aware batching, strategy that groups tasks according to their measured fragility. It reduces generated tokens by 43% across all datasets while preserving accuracy on both state-of-the-art open-weight models and proprietary frontier models (Section 4).

sections.title: 2 Preliminaries
sections.content: Our central goal is to investigate whether an LLM that can solve task in isolation keeps this ability when several such tasks are presented together. To answer this, we use controlled setting in which the constituent tasks are unchanged and only the number of tasks in the prompt varies. We then measure how each tasks accuracy changes relative to its performance in isolation. All experiments share the setup described below. Compositions. We compose independent tasks drawn from the same dataset D. composition of size is tuple = (t1, . . . , tk) with ti D, rendered into single prompt by fixed per-dataset template that asks the model to answer all tasks in order. We split the models single response into answers and grade each for correctness (further details in Appendix A.2.6). Accuracy drop. For model m, the accuracy drop of each individual task ti at composition size is (1), where negative values indicate degradation. Unless stated otherwise, accuracy is estimated from 5 independent trials. (k) = accm (k) accm Datasets. We use eight datasets whose tasks vary widely in the reasoning they require. We build two datasets ourselves: 1,000 indefinite integrals with randomized coefficients across diverse function classes, verified symbolically, and OneWordQA, set of factual questions with single-word or numeric answers that require minimal reasoning. The remaining six are established benchmarks: GPQA-Diamond [Rein et al., 2023], GSM8K [Cobbe et al., 2021], MATH-500 [Hendrycks et al., 2021, Lightman et al., 2023], MMLURedux [Gema et al., 2025], StrategyQA [Geva et al., 2021] and AIME (further details in Appendix A.2.6). Models. We evaluate three Qwen3 models (4B Thinking, 8B, 14B) [Yang et al., 2025a], trained by strongto-weak distillation from larger RL-trained Qwen3 models, and Qwen3.8 27B [Qwen Team, 2026]. We also evaluate three DeepSeek-R1-distilled models (Qwen 7B, Llama 8B, Qwen3 8B) [Guo et al., 2025], obtained by supervised fine-tuning on R1 reasoning traces, and the frontier model Claude Opus 5 with medium reasoning effort. The first two groups let us compare two different post-training recipes at similar scale. Open-weight models are sampled at temperature 0.6 and use context limit of at least 131,072 tokens (further details in Appendix A.2.2).

sections.title: 3 Composing tasks causes performance degradation
sections.content: Prior work has repeatedly reported that accuracy falls when several tasks share single prompt. However, these evaluations do not isolate whether model fails because it cannot solve task reliably or purely because the task is composed with others, which leaves the underlying mechanism unclear. Building on these observations, we ask whether degradation can arise from composition alone. Answering this requires separating models ability to solve task from its ability to solve the same task in composition. For that, we restrict each model to subset DM of confidently solved tasks: task enters DM only if solves it in isolation in three out of three independent attempts. We then build 3 compositions of size {3, 6, 10, 20}* exclusively from DM, sampling task categories uniformly within each dataset, and evaluate the accuracy of each task within them. The accuracies at = 1 come from runs independent of those used for selection. Figure 2: Accuracy degradation on confidently solved GPQA-Diamond tasks. Left: accuracy drop per model at = 10. Right: accuracy drop as function of composition size k. All tasks were solved in three out of three isolated attempts, yet accuracy drops once they are composed. As Figure 2 shows, simply concatenating tasks that are solvable in isolation causes substantial accuracy degradation across all models on GPQA-Diamond [Rein et al., 2023]. This observation also holds for all other datasets we tested, except OneWordQA and StrategyQA, whose tasks require little reasoning. Furthermore, this degradation cannot be explained by context-length issues, since nearly all responses stay within the context limit (see Figure 3 and Appendix A.1.1). Compositional degradation is therefore driven by effects inherent to composition and cannot be predicted from the solvability of tasks in isolation alone. The extent of this degradation varies strongly across models. The R1-distilled models degrade the most, while the Qwen3 models degrade moderately less. Frontier models are not immune either: Claude Opus 5, despite its leading benchmark results, loses about 7 pp at = 10 on GPQA-Diamond, on tasks it solved in all three runs individually. Figure 3: Context usage across datasets. Most responses use under 25% of the context window; in most datasets, under 1% hit the limit. Contrary to explanations for compositions with dependent tasks, where models either match solution patterns seen in training instead of learning systematic procedures [Dziri et al., 2023] or fail to combine facts they know individually [Press et al., 2023], we propose that compositional degradation arises from misallocation of the implicit thinking budget.

sections.title: 3.2 Fragile tasks are stable within a model
sections.content: It remains to establish whether the implicit thinking budget estimation fails consistently on the same tasks across models and composition sizes. This tells us how the proposed misallocation changes as the conditions, i.e., model and composition size, vary. Since failure in implicit thinking budget estimation manifests as accuracy degradation, we can test this consistency directly on the accuracy drops. For two conditions and B, we obtain the accuracy drops across tasks, and B, and measure their Pearson correlation, applying Spearmans correction for attenuation to reduce the impact of noisy accuracy estimates (details in Appendix A.2.3). At fixed composition size, the mean correlation across models is only 0.24 0.03. Different models thus largely disagree on which tasks degrade, even when evaluated under identical conditions. The exception is models trained with the same recipe, such as Qwen3 8B and 14B, which correlate at 0.56 0.09. Within single model, the correlation across composition sizes reaches 0.81 0.04. When the same model faces compositions of different sizes, groupings and orderings, the same set of fragile tasks tends to break. Fragility is therefore stable property of task for given model. Measuring tasks accuracy drop at some composition sizes lets us anticipate how it will degrade in new compositions presented to the same model, which makes fragility predictable.

(3) We find λ by grid search on held-out splits, using repeated nested 5-fold cross-validation [Cawley and Talbot, 2010] to reduce the effect of noise in the empirical accuracy estimates. Given the assignments ki(λ), we greedily group tasks into as few compositions as possible such that every task ti lands in composition with ki(λ) (details in Appendix A.2.4). Throughout our experiments, we use the composition sizes = {1, 3, 6, 10, 20}, where = 1 solves task alone, and an accuracy drop budget of = 0.5%. Table 1 compares the accuracy degradation and token savings of different batching strategies relative to solving tasks in isolation. The common practice of batching tasks randomly into fixed-size compositions [Cheng et al., 2023], here of six tasks, saves the most tokens on average but degrades accuracy strongly, particularly on GPQA-Diamond, whose tasks require many reasoning steps. Fragility-aware batching almost entirely avoids this degradation while still achieving substantial token savings. Averaged over all models and over every dataset but AIME, where fragility-aware batching leaves nearly every task in isolation (Appendix A.1.6), it saves 43% of tokens while keeping accuracy constant (+0.6 pp). How these savings arise depends on the dataset. On OneWordQA and StrategyQA, fragility-aware batching matches random batching, saving 6874% of output tokens without losing accuracy relative to solving each task individually. On the remaining five datasets, where random batching degrades accuracy, fragility-aware batching preserves it while still saving roughly 32%. These results show that much of the thinking an LLM spends on task in isolation is not needed to solve it. Specifically, on GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K and MMLU-Redux, grouping tasks by fragility saves substantial share of tokens at no cost in accuracy.

sections.title: 4.2 Predicting fragility on held-out tasks
sections.content: Our results show that the set of fragile tasks is stable for given model, which hints at the existence of steady properties that define fragility. If such properties exist, fragility should be predictable for tasks the model has never seen under composition. Hence, we extend the intervention to unseen tasks by predicting their fragility with simple linear predictor. We encode each task description with Qwen3 Embedding 8B [Zhang et al., 2025], keep the embeddings fixed, and train separate linear predictor for each evaluated language model. To generate labels, we evaluate each task in the training split with 10 trials at every composition size {3, 6, 10, 20}, placing it in different composition each time. Then, for each composition size the predictor outputs the probability that the task performs at least as well in composition as in isolation. To obtain predictions on unseen tasks, we use 5-fold cross-fitting [Chernozhukov et al., 2024], so that the held-out folds together cover the entire dataset (details in Appendix A.2.5). Finally, we feed the predicted accuracy drops into the same batching algorithm as in Section 4.1. Table 1 reports the results of the linear predictor. Guided by the predictor, fragility-aware batching limits the accuracy loss to at most 0.5 pp on every dataset and saves 31.0% of tokens on average. Because few training examples are available, the predictor is simple, and it works best on tasks with short, plain 8 descriptions such as Integrals, GSM8K and OneWordQA. This simple demonstration thus shows that fragility is partly predictable from task properties encoded in the embeddings. Scaling such predictors further could enable saving tokens on real-world unseen tasks, just by batching them well. Fragility-aware batching on frontier model. We further test whether fragility-aware batching carries over to flagship frontier LLMs. Since the intervention requires neither fine-tuning nor access to internal states and works purely by restructuring compositions, we can apply it directly to Claude Opus 5 on GPQA-Diamond  (Table 1)  . In isolation, Claude Opus 5 reaches an accuracy of 89.5% with 689 output tokens per task. Random composition with k=6 lowers accuracy by 0.9 pp and saves 18% of output tokens. Batching by measured fragility does better on both metrics, losing just 0.4 pp while saving 24% of generated tokens. The linear predictor, trained on fewer trials for Opus than for the open-weight models, transfers less well: it saves almost no tokens and loses 2.0 pp. At least in its consequences, the mechanism we found in open-weight models carries over to frontier model.

sections.title: 5 Effects of post-training on compositional degradation
sections.content: Figure 6: Effects of implicit budgeting across three post-training stages of OLMo 3 7B on GPQA-Diamond. Left: Token ratio ri(k) = Ti(k)/Ti(1) as function of composition size k. Right: Accuracy drop as function of the token ratio. The models in our analysis degrade very differently under composition, most clearly between the two model families, which differ in their post-training strategy. This hints that post-training strongly influences how well model handles compositions. To investigate this, we repeat our analysis on OLMo 3 7B [Olmo et al., 2026] at three stages of its training curriculum: SFT [Ouyang et al., 2022], DPO [Rafailov et al., 2024] and RLVR [Lambert et al., 2025, Guo et al., 2025]. Figure 6 summarizes the results on OLMo 3 7B. All three stages show very similar implicit budgeting under composition, and their token counts shrink at similar rates. Nevertheless, the same reduction affects accuracy differently. At similar token ratios, the final RLVR stage loses substantially less accuracy than the SFT and DPO stages. These degrade by similar amounts and also tend to fail on the same fragile tasks. Correlating their accuracy degradation on GPQA-Diamond, MATH-500 and MMLU-Redux as in Section 3.2 gives disattenuated Pearson ρ of 1.03 0.35. RLVRs fragile set tends to overlap less with theirs, with ρ = 0.69 0.23 against SFT and ρ = 0.89 0.26 against DPO. We conclude that RLVR post-training mitigates the accuracy drop incurred by implicit budgeting under composition, but it does not eliminate the misallocation of the thinking budget in the first place, which remained similar across the stages.

sections.title: 6 Related work
sections.content: Previous work has examined both how task composition affects accuracy and reasoning length and how batching can improve efficiency or reliability. Several studies ask whether models can solve tasks as reliably together as they do separately [Pan et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025, Chen et al., 2026]. Related studies examine whether failures to meet multiple response requirements can be explained by independent errors [Harada et al., 2025, Vasileva, 2026]. These studies document accuracy losses under composition, although their causes are not yet fully understood. At the same time, batching methods have shown promise for improving efficiency and reliability [Xu et al., 2026a, Ji et al., 2025], with accuracy gains reported in some settings [Srivastava et al., 2026, Yang et al., 2026b, Lin et al., 2024] (consistent with our observations on light-reasoning datasets OneWordQA and StrategyQA, see Appendix A.1.6). Batching has also been observed to reduce the number of reasoning tokens used per task [Srivastava et al., 2026, Deng et al., 2026]. The effects of added context also vary across questions. For factual questions, models tend to resist misleading information more successfully when they can also answer related questions correctly, suggesting that accuracy in isolation does not fully capture robustness [Xu et al., 2026b]. The number of steps needed to solve task also matters. Tasks requiring more steps show larger accuracy drops when irrelevant information is added [Yang et al., 2025b]. More broadly, researchers distinguish task difficulty from sensitivity to prompt changes [Romanou et al., 2026] and examine how that sensitivity varies with model size, training and architecture [Qin et al., 2026]. Overall accuracy can remain largely unchanged even when irrelevant context changes which questions model answers correctly [Zhang et al., 2026]. Estimates of this sensitivity also depend on how answers are graded. Rigid matching rules can treat differently worded correct answers as errors, exaggerating the apparent sensitivity [Hua et al., 2025]. Alongside these studies, work on reasoning allocation has shown that adding other tasks or irrelevant text can shorten reasoning traces and reduce self-checking [Rodionov et al., 2026]. Researchers have also trained models to solve groups of tasks more efficiently under shared token limit [Yang et al., 2026a]. However, studies of budget allocation find that models often devote more reasoning to earlier questions than to those worth more points [Fan et al., 2026]. In single-task setting, model confidence has also been used to guide search for shorter reasoning paths [Huang et al., 2026]. These findings can be difficult to reconcile within common explanation, given the differences in experimental settings, interventions and datasets. Our work offers unifying perspective on several of these observations. Budget misallocation is consistent with the greater sensitivity of deeper reasoning tasks to irrelevant context [Yang et al., 2025b], self-compression [Deng et al., 2026], composition errors that cannot be explained by independent error rates alone [Harada et al., 2025], and the token savings achieved through batching [Srivastava et al., 2026, Cheng et al., 2023]. We identify reasoning trace length in isolation as key variable that helps connect these findings and informs simple, effective interventions. Using this information, we are able to show how to mitigate degradation under composition, even in frontier models.

sections.title: 7 Discussion and conclusions
sections.content: In this work, we show that language models fail on tasks they solve reliably in isolation once those tasks are combined in single prompt. The resulting accuracy drop is larger than expected from isolated error rates alone. As more tasks are combined, models use fewer reasoning tokens per task, following an approximate power-law decay with composition size, and the largest failures occur on tasks that require longer reasoning in isolation. This reveals an implicit per-task budget that acts as double-edged sword. Under composition, fragile tasks receive too little reasoning and fail. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. By batching tasks according to their fragility, however, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by about 43% on average while preserving accuracy, and since it does not require internal states of the model, it also applies to proprietary models such as Claude Opus 5. 10 Previous context can cause degradation too. We deliberately compose independent tasks of the same type, isolating the budget effect in its simplest form. An important question is how this effect extends to richer contexts. Prior work finds that reasoning traces also shorten when the same task is embedded in irrelevant context, conversation history, or larger task [Rodionov et al., 2026], suggesting that implicit thinking budgeting may extend beyond same-type composition. Long-running agents in production. This is particularly relevant to agentic workflows, where tool outputs, interaction histories, and intermediate results continually accumulate. Agents are widely observed to degrade as their context grows, phenomenon known as context rot [Hong et al., 2025]. Our results point to degradation that sets in long before the context fills up. In an agentic workflow, this means high-effort step can be unknowingly misbudgeted, thus possibly leading to error propagation in subsequent tasks. As direct practical intervention, agents can keep their context lean and hand reasoning-intensive steps to subagents that start from fresh context. Post-training as potential mitigation. Our results suggest that reasoning allocation contributes to the difficulty of composed tasks, even when the constituent tasks are solvable in isolation. Post-training may therefore help mitigate degradation under composition. For instance, integrating budget management into RL pipelines through explicit training on composed tasks could help models allocate reasoning more effectively across shared prompt. Limitations. While we show that composition systematically reduces per-task reasoning and disproportionately harms fragile tasks, we do not yet know what drives this reduction. Our study is limited to independent, same-dataset compositions, and detailed reasoning-length analysis is restricted to openweight models. Extending these results to mixed-domain, dependent, and proprietary-model settings remains important future work.

sections.content: A.1 Further results A.1.1 Compositional degradation is observable over wide range of datasets and models Figure 7: Accuracy drop as function of composition size for all datasets and models. All tasks were solved in three out of three isolated attempts, yet accuracy drops once they are composed, on every dataset except OneWordQA and StrategyQA, whose tasks require little reasoning. The R1-distilled models degrade the most, and the extent of degradation varies strongly between datasets. Compositional degradation is not caused by context length or parsing. Since composed tasks require more context and use different answer format than isolated tasks, two natural confounders of compositional degradation are truncation due to context overflow and failures in parsing the composed answer. The results in Table 3 show that neither factor accounts for the observed degradation. Context length poses little difficulty: in most datasets, fewer than 1% of responses reach the context limit, even at the largest we evaluate. Parsing failures are likewise rare across all datasets except AIME. There, the majority of these failures arise because the model returns fewer answers than there are tasks, which itself constitutes failure to solve the composition. A.1.2 Composition size influences token ratio Figures 814 show the token ratio ri(k) = Ti(k)/Ti(1) as function of composition size for all seven open-weight models. Tasks are binned by the quantile of their isolated trace length into Low ( 20%), 16 Medium (2080%), and High (> 80%). On log-log axes, the ratio decreases approximately linearly in log for nearly all models and datasets, indicating that LLMs shrink the relative token usage of each task under composition by km. The exception is R1 Qwen 7B on MATH-500, where the ratio of the Low bin rises above 1 and the fit over all tasks is flat (m = 0.04, R2 = 0.43). This reduction shows no systematic dependence on Ti(1), since the ordering of the length bins varies across models and datasets and no bin is consistently reduced more than the others. We fix each power-law fit to pass through (1, 1), since composition of single task has token ratio of 1 by construction. Each caption summarizes the six fits of model, one per dataset over all of its tasks, by the median and range of the slope and the mean R2. Figure 8: Token ratio on Qwen3 4B Thinking. In each plot, tasks are binned by the quantile of their isolated thinking length Ti(1) into Low ( 20%), Medium (2080%), and High (> 80%), and the accuracy drop is shown as function of the relative thinking token reduction. Below the dashed line, the y-axis is logarithmic. The pattern holds across all models. Accuracy drops as the reduction grows, and in most cases tasks with long isolated thinking traces degrade substantially more than tasks with short ones. Figure 21: Accuracy drop versus relative thinking token reduction for R1 Qwen3 8B. 24 Budget forcing causes degradation analogous to composition. To rule out possible context effects, we take the budget task receives when it is solved in composition and apply it to the same task solved in isolation. Following Muennighoff et al. [2025], we inject </think> once the thinking trace reaches this budget. In composition, the model also spends tokens on restating the question and checking the output format. To cover this constant overhead, we add the full share of unattributed tokens (tokens not attributed to any task) from the composed solution to the budget. Figures 5 and 1521 show the results as forced. We find that stopping the thinking abruptly causes substantially larger degradation than the planned reduction of thinking tokens under composition. Still, the same pattern emerges. Degradation rises monotonically as the budget shrinks, and tasks with higher reasoning requirements, measured by their thinking length in isolation, consistently degrade more than tasks with low requirements. In terms of its effect on accuracy, composing tasks therefore appears to act analogously to forcing budget. A.2 Methodological details A.2.1 Measuring per-task thinking length To measure how model divides its thinking across the tasks of composition, we prefix each task with unique tag (Q01, Q02, . . . ) and instruct the model to name the tag whenever it turns to that task. The tags mark where the reasoning on one task ends and the next begins. We assign every token after tag to the corresponding task, up to the next tag or the end of the thinking trace. The thinking length Ti(k) of task ti in composition of size is the total number of tokens assigned to it, and the model may return to task more than once. task that is never named receives no tokens. dual catalyst system for ethylene polymerization ... tentatively D. <think> Q01: The dye emits light with an energy of 2.34 eV ... maybe A. Q02: Back to Q01: 2.34 eV is about 530 nm, so the absorbed light ... B. Q03: ... </think> Here the tokens after both Q01 tags count towards t1, while t2 receives the tokens between its tag and the second Q01. This rule cannot reliably find where the trace for the last question in composition ends, since no next tag marks its end, so its length is often overestimated. To fix this, we append an ungraded dummy question at the end of each composition. In our experiments, this tagging strategy works quite well: LLMs name every task in 99.5% of all tagged thinking traces. We generate the integral pool ourselves, to ensure that every problem is known to be solvable and simple enough for most small open-weight models to solve confidently. It holds 1,000 atomic integrands, 200 from each of five function classes: polynomial: xn; exponential: ebx; trigonometric: (bx + c) with {sin, cos, tan}; logarithmic and rational: ln(bx + c) or a/(bx + c); integration by parts: (bx + c) with {exp, sin, cos, ln, arctan}. The coefficient is nonzero integer in [5, 5]. The exponent and the frequency are nonzero integers in [15, 15], and the shift is an integer in [15, 15]. All parameters are drawn with fixed seed. Structural duplicates are discarded. An integrand is kept only if SymPy finds an elementary antiderivative for it, and only if that antiderivative passes the same checker that grades the models. The checker works symbolically rather than by string matching. It parses the boxed LaTeX answer, differentiates it, and tests whether the derivative equals the integrand, first structurally, then numerically at random points, and finally with symbolic proof under timeout. An additive constant is accepted, but any other free symbol is rejected. Answers that cannot be parsed, or whose check times out, are recorded separately rather than counted as wrong. OneWordQA. OneWordQA is set of 1,548 questions that we generated using Claude Opus 5 and checked manually. They cover 23 categories of simple factual lookups whose answers leave little room for interpretation. Examples include country capitals, dialing and ISO codes, chemical symbols and atomic numbers, Roman numerals, polygon sides and the number of players per team in sport. Each answer is single word, number or short code. Grading normalizes only how an answer is written (case, diacritics and surrounding punctuation). Where question has more than one correct answer, the alternatives are listed explicitly in the dataset. Benchmarks. The six public benchmarks are loaded from the Hugging Face Hub at pinned revisions. We use the error-free questions of MMLU-Redux, drawing the same number from each of 19 subjects (74 per subject, 1,406 questions), and keep the answer options in their published order. GPQA-Diamond contributes 196 of its 198 questions; we drop the two that repeat an answer option. From GSM8K we take the 1,319 problems of the test split, from MATH-500 all 500 problems, and from AIME the 60 problems of 2024 and 2025. StrategyQA contributes the 687 questions of its test split, and an answer counts as correct when it is the gold yes or no. Prompts.
